abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are the standard first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant cancer (non-small cell lung cancer [NSCLC]), achieving an objective response rate (ORR) of approximately 60%–70%. However, optimizing their therapeutic efficacy remains a challenge. NSCLC cells express the tumor-specific hypoglycosylated Thomsen-nouvelle (Tn) mucin 1 (MUC1) antigen, making them suitable targets for TnMUC1 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy. This study shows that EGFR TKIs enhance the efficacy of TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, both in vitro and in vivo. EGFR TKIs upregulate TnMUC1 by reducing MUC1 glycosylation, thereby improving TnMUC1 CAR-T cell recognition and cytotoxicity. Specifically, EGFR TKIs modulate TnMUC1-related glycosyltransferases, with core1-beta1,3-galactosyltransferase 1 (C1GALT1) identified as a key enzyme downregulated by EGFR TKIs, suggesting C1GALT1 as a potential therapeutic target.

abstract.p: Zhou et al. show that EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors enhance TnMUC1 CAR-T cell efficacy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC by suppressing C1GALT1 via PI3K/AKT/SP1 signaling, thereby reducing MUC1 glycosylation and promoting antigen exposure, and propose a combination strategy to improve targeted and immunotherapeutic outcomes.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: In recent years, significant advancements have reshaped the treatment landscape of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). While chemotherapy remains a cornerstone, targeted therapies have revolutionized care by providing precise interventions for tumors with specific genetic mutations. Additionally, immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have emerged as powerful therapeutic options, further expanding the arsenal of treatments against lung cancer.

For patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutant NSCLC, EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs) are the standard first-line treatment. Clinical trials, such as ENSURE III and AURA17, have shown that EGFR TKIs (e.g., erlotinib and osimertinib) can achieve objective response rates (ORRs) of approximately 62.7%–63% in Asian populations.1,2 Nearly 40% of EGFR-mutant patients, however, exhibit primary resistance, particularly those who have TP53 mutations or MET amplification.1,2,3,4 Additionally, even with the most effective third-generation EGFR TKIs, median progression-free survival (PFS) remains limited to approximately 18.9 months.5 Resistance to first-line osimertinib is heterogeneous and often untargetable, thus driving research toward combination therapies that may enhance long-term efficacy. Combination therapy strategies generally target tumor cells by integrating EGFR TKIs with chemotherapy or other targeted agents. For example, combining EGFR TKIs with platinum-based chemotherapy (FLAURA2 study)6 extends PFS by approximately 1.5-fold; however, this treatment more than doubles the incidence of adverse events (AEs). EGFR TKIs combined with anti-angiogenic agents, such as osimertinib plus bevacizumab (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04181060)7 or osimertinib plus ramucirumab (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03909334, JapicCTI-184146), show minimal PFS improvement but increase the incidence of anti-angiogenesis-related toxicities, including hypertension and proteinuria. Another treatment approach involves evanvorvimab, an EGFR/mesenchymal-epithelial transition factor (c-MET) bispecific antibody, with or without lazertinib or osimertinib. Compared with osimertinib alone, evanvorvimab plus lazertinib extended PFS by more than 1.5-fold; however, 75% of patients experienced AEs (grade 3 or higher), and 50% developed serious AEs (SAEs). Despite these strategies, the emergence of resistant tumor clones ultimately leads to disease progression.

From the perspective of the tumor microenvironment, immunotherapy has emerged as a potential strategy for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Its efficacy remains uncertain, however.8,9 According to the Impower010 trial, adjuvant atezolizumab did not translate into an overall survival (OS) benefit for patients who had EGFR mutations.10 This finding suggests that EGFR mutation status is a critical negative predictive factor for immunotherapy, and patients with EGFR mutations should avoid such treatment approaches. Similarly, ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02879994, a phase 2 clinical trial, evaluated the efficacy and safety of pembrolizumab (a PD-1 inhibitor) monotherapy as a first-line treatment for EGFR-mutant NSCLC.8 The trial data demonstrated that, regardless of PD-L1 expression status, the ORR of EGFR-mutant NSCLC to PD-1 monotherapy was generally low (<20%), and PFS benefits were limited. These findings suggest that PD-1 monotherapy may not be sufficient to overcome the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment in this patient population. In the first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC, combining EGFR TKIs with ICIs has not demonstrated a clear survival benefit and has posed significant toxicity risks.11,12,13,14 This toxicity has hindered the clinical application of EGFR TKIs in combination with ICIs for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Consequently, novel immunotherapeutic strategies warrant further investigation for EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

Mucin 1 (MUC1) is a highly glycosylated transmembrane protein, but its glycosylation levels are abnormally low in tumor cells, distinguishing them from normal cells. The Thomsen-nouvelle (Tn) antigen consists of an O-glycosidic-linked N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) attached to the hydroxyl (-OH) group of serine (S) or threonine (T).15 Specifically, the Tn glycoform of MUC1 (TnMUC1) is a tumor-specific antigen (TSA) that has shown promising diagnostic and therapeutic potential in adenocarcinomas.16,17,18,19,20 Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has demonstrated significant potential in treating NSCLC. The overexpression of MUC1 in lung cancer cells positions MUC1-targeted CAR-T cells as a viable therapeutic strategy to treat NSCLC (Figure S1).21 A phase 1 clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03525782) evaluating MUC1-targeted CAR-T cells in advanced NSCLC has reported substantial primary tumor regression, but it also found limited efficacy against metastatic lesions. Preclinically, TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T cells induced robust tumor rejection and prolonged survival in disseminated cancer models, mediated by the high tumor-restricted expression of the TnMUC1 glycoform.22 CAR-T cell therapy, however, has encountered limited success in treating solid tumors. Notably, studies have demonstrated that EGFR frequently interacts with MUC1 to promote tumor progression.23,24,25 Therefore, we proposed a therapeutic strategy to combine EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. Our results demonstrated that EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells exert synergistic anticancer effects both in vivo and in vitro. Notably, safety assessments in patient-derived xenografts (PDXs) revealed no significant abnormalities in organ function after combined osimertinib and TnMUC1 CAR-T cell treatment (Figure S5). Collectively, these findings indicated that the combination of EGFR TKIs and immunotherapy is both safe and effective.

Mechanistically, EGFR TKIs reduced MUC1 glycosylation levels, thereby enhancing TnMUC1 antigen exposure and facilitating recognition and cytotoxicity by TnMUC1 CAR-T cells. We identified core1-beta1,3-galactosyltransferase 1 (C1GALT1) as a key glycosyltransferase involved in TnMUC1 glycosylation. EGFR TKIs suppressed C1GALT1 transcription through the PI3K/AKT/SP1 pathway. Furthermore, C1GALT1 inhibitors, such as itraconazole, directly reduced MUC1 glycosylation and promoted TnMUC1 expression. On the basis of these findings, we proposed a combination strategy incorporating EGFR and C1GALT1 inhibitors with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells to enhance the clinical efficacy of targeted therapy and immunotherapy for NSCLC. The results of this study suggested that combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells is a promising therapeutic strategy for EGFR-mutant NSCLC. A major challenge in CAR-T cell therapy for solid tumors is the limited availability of suitable antigens, as tumor cells may lack or express low levels of the target antigen.26,27 In this study, we proposed an approach in which EGFR TKIs can be repurposed not for their conventional role in inhibiting tumor growth through EGFR signaling but rather to upregulate the tumor-associated antigen MUC1, thereby enhancing TnMUC1 CAR-T cell recognition and cytotoxicity. This strategy differentiates this study from traditional EGFR TKI applications and EGFR TKI and ICI combinations.

sec.title: Combined administration of EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells achieves tumor suppression in xenograft models
sec.p:
EGFR TKIs are standard first-line treatments for EGFR-mutant NSCLC, but their efficacy remains limited. To enhance therapeutic outcomes, we combined EGFR TKIs with MUC1-targeted CAR-T cell therapy. Despite advances in MUC1 CAR-T development, clinical efficacy has been limited, largely due to low target antigen expression in solid tumors.28,29 To investigate the expression level of TnMUC1 in NSCLC, we evaluated TnMUC1 expression in NSCLC clinical specimens through immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis. Because of the unavailability of commercial TnMUC1-specific antibodies, we utilized the Tn218 antibody, which was generated using asialo ovine submaxillary mucin (aOSM), to detect TnMUC1 expression. To validate the specificity of the Tn218 antibody for the Tn antigen exclusively on MUC1 protein, we performed a pull-down assay using PC9 cells (harboring EGFR exon 19 deletion) and HCC827 cells (with EGFR exon 19 deletion) (Figure S2). Our results demonstrated that Tn218 specifically recognized the Tn epitope on MUC1 without cross-reactivity to Tn antigens on other proteins, confirming its reliability for assessing TnMUC1 expression levels. The IHC analysis of TnMUC1 using the Tn218 antibody revealed generally low expression levels in NSCLC samples, regardless of their EGFR mutation status (Figures 1A and 1B). This finding may explain the limited efficacy observed in current TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T cell therapies. Notably, we identified elevated TnMUC1 antigen expression in a subset of patients harboring EGFR mutations, which indicated a potential therapeutic subgroup that may derive a benefit from TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T cell therapies. Considering the well-established interaction between EGFR and MUC1 in cancer progression, we conducted a comprehensive correlation analysis utilizing The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database. Our analysis did not reveal a significant association between EGFR and MUC1 mRNA expression levels in EGFR wild-type NSCLC (Figure 1C). We detected, however, a statistically significant correlation between EGFR and MUC1 expression in EGFR-mutant NSCLC cases (Figure 1D). To further elucidate the functional consequences of this relationship, we performed MUC1-knockdown experiments in PC9 cells followed by osimertinib treatment. Cell proliferation assays revealed that osimertinib monotherapy reduced cell viability by approximately 60% following a 48-h treatment period, whereas MUC1 knockdown potentiated this effect, resulting in an 80% reduction in cell viability (Figure S3A). These results suggest that a synergistic antitumor effect was achieved through combined EGFR TKI therapy and MUC1 inhibition.Figure 1

Because EGFR interacts with MUC1 to promote tumor growth, we investigated whether EGFR TKIs combined with TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy could produce a synergistic effect. To test this hypothesis, we performed in vivo experiments using both first-generation (erlotinib) and third-generation (osimertinib) EGFR TKIs. We established cell-derived xenografts (CDXs) by subcutaneously injecting PC9 or HCC827 cells into NOD.Cg-PrkdcscidIl2rgem1Smoc (NSG) immunocompromised mice. To assess whether EGFR TKIs could be administered simultaneously with TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy, we investigated the effects of EGFR TKIs on T cell activation. We treated peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) with 1 μM erlotinib or osimertinib, followed by evaluation of interleukin-2 (IL-2) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) release after activation using an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA; Figures S3B and S3C) and analysis of CD25+CD8+ and CD69+CD8+ T cell populations through flow cytometry (Figures S3D–S3G). These results demonstrate that neither erlotinib nor osimertinib suppressed T cell activation. These findings support the compatibility of combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells in therapeutic strategies. In subcutaneous tumor models using PC9 cells (Figures 1E and 1F) and HCC827 cells (Figures 1G and 1H), combination therapy with EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells achieved more than 75% tumor volume reduction. In contrast, monotherapy with either erlotinib or osimertinib resulted in approximately 50% tumor reduction, and TnMUC1 CAR-T cell treatment alone showed less than 20% efficacy compared with controls. To evaluate the durability of the combined therapeutic effect, we established osimertinib-resistant HCC827 cells (HCC827-OR) through prolonged in vitro exposure to 100 nM osimertinib for 30 days (Figure S4A). Subsequently, we implanted HCC827-OR cells into NSG mice. TnMUC1 CAR-T cell monotherapy reduced tumor volume by more than 50%, whereas osimertinib treatment alone showed limited efficacy (about a 30% reduction), likely because of acquired resistance. Notably, the combination therapy induced near-complete tumor regression, demonstrating its superior antitumor activity (Figures S4B and S4C).

To validate the combined efficacy of EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells in preclinical models, we established PDXs using tumor tissues from three patients with lung cancer who were harboring EGFR exon 19 deletions. Following the established treatment regimen, we administered osimertinib in combination with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells. The combination therapy group demonstrated near-complete tumor regression, whereas the osimertinib monotherapy group showed a reduction of more than 60% tumor volume. TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy alone achieved a tumor reduction of approximately 40% (Figures 1I–1N), which was consistent across all three PDX models despite their varying growth rates. These in vivo findings confirm that the combination of EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy produces superior therapeutic outcomes in EGFR-mutant NSCLC.

To evaluate the safety of the combination therapy involving EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells, we analyzed plasma samples from PDX models following treatment. We performed hematological and biochemical tests, including red blood cell, platelet, transaminases, bilirubin, creatinine, urea, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, and amylase (Figure S5A). We also conducted histopathological assessments of spleen, lung, liver, kidney, and heart tissues using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Figure S5B). We did not detect any significant abnormalities in serum biomarkers or organ histology, which indicated that the combined regimen of osimertinib and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells demonstrated preliminary safety.

To elucidate the underlying mechanisms of combination therapy efficacy, we investigated whether the observed effects were primarily mediated by CAR-T cell cytotoxicity or osimertinib-induced tumor regression. On the basis of our previous tumor cell proliferation experiments involving EGFR TKIs and MUC1 knockdown, we observed that MUC1 knockdown alone did not produce a significant antitumor effect with EGFR TKIs. Therefore, we hypothesized that EGFR TKIs primarily enhanced the cytotoxic activity of CAR-T cells. Then, we quantified IFN-γ levels in tumor tissue lysates using an ELISA (Figure 1O) because IFN-γ represented a crucial cytokine for T cell-mediated cytotoxicity and thus served as a reliable biomarker for both PBMCs and CAR-T cell activity. Our analysis revealed significantly elevated IFN-γ levels in the combination therapy group compared with the groups treated with PBMCs or TnMUC1 monotherapy. IHC analysis of CD3 expression demonstrated enhanced CAR-T cell infiltration in tumor tissues following osimertinib treatment (Figures 1P and 1Q). These results indicate that the therapeutic synergy extends beyond the tumor-suppressive effects of EGFR TKIs, with osimertinib additionally potentiating the antitumor activity of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells.

sec.title: EGFR TKIs potentiate TnMUC1 CAR-T cell cytotoxic activity in in vitro coculture models
sec.p:
To investigate the cytotoxic effects of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells, we established a coculture system with tumor cells (Figures 2A, 2B, S6A, and S6B). Cytotoxicity assays demonstrated that although either EGFR TKIs or TnMUC1 CAR-T cells alone moderately increased tumor cell death, their combination significantly enhanced tumor cell lysis. This finding was further supported by a lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) release assay (Figure S6C). These findings suggested that EGFR TKIs enhanced the antitumor immune response by potentiating the cytotoxicity of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells. To investigate whether the tumor cell death observed during the 8-h coculture treatment was mediated by PBMCs or CAR-T cells rather than by EGFR TKIs, we quantified the death ratio of PC9 and HCC827 cells following treatment with erlotinib or osimertinib. After 8 h of exposure, neither erlotinib nor osimertinib induced significant cell death in PC9 or HCC827 cells (Figures 2C–2F), which confirmed that the cytotoxic effects in the coculture system were mediated primarily by PBMCs or CAR-T cells.Figure 2

Additionally, we assessed tumor cell survival in the coculture system, using CD45 as a marker for immune cells. We identified tumor cells as CD45-negative and calcein-positive cells (Figures 2G and 2H). The results showed that the combination of osimertinib and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells reduced tumor cell survival to less than half of that observed with either treatment alone. However, the cell proliferation assay assessing osimertinib treatment of PC9 and HCC827 cells showed that osimertinib did not reduce the tumor cell count within 8 h (Figure S3A). This result suggests that the reduction in viable tumor cells during the 8-h coculture treatment was due to the lysis by PBMCs or CAR-T cells rather than the inhibition of EGFR TKI.

To investigate the functional roles of PBMCs or TnMUC1 CAR-T cells in cocultures, we quantified the concentrations of IFN-γ (Figures 2I and S6D) and granzyme B (GZMB) (Figure 2J) in the coculture supernatants, as these cytokines are critical mediators of T cell cytotoxic activity. Additionally, to evaluate the functional state of immune cells during coculture, we measured levels of immunosuppressive cytokines, including transforming growth factor β (TGF-β; Figure S6E) and IL-10 (Figure S6F), in the supernatants. The results showed that osimertinib treatment of PC9 cells induced a 1.5-fold increase in IFN-γ release by PBMCs, while it induced a more than 4-fold increase in IFN-γ release by CAR-T cells. Similarly, osimertinib treatment of HCC827 cells resulted in a greater than 3-fold increase in IFN-γ release by PBMCs, whereas cotreatment with CAR-T cells led to a more than 6-fold increase in IFN-γ release compared with PBMCs alone. The ELISA results for GZMB were consistent with those for IFN-γ. In contrast, when cocultured with PBMCs, we observed that osimertinib treatment of PC9 and HCC827 cells reduced TGF-β levels in the culture medium by 50%. When cocultured with CAR-T cells, osimertinib further reduced TGF-β levels by 75%, which could be attributed to the decrease in tumor cell count and the inhibitory effect of EGFR TKIs on tumor cell TGF-β secretion. Additionally, compared with PBMCs, coculturing CAR-T cells with PC9 and HCC827 cells resulted in a significant reduction in IL-10 levels in the culture medium, which may have reflected the less immunosuppressive nature of CAR-T cells. The combined decline in TGF-β and IL-10 levels correlated with enhanced T cell cytotoxic activity, suggesting that cytokine modulation contributed to the improved antitumor efficacy.

These in vitro experiments demonstrate that EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells have enhanced anticancer effects when used in combination. During coculture, EGFR TKIs significantly increased the cytotoxicity of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells.

sec.title: EGFR TKIs downregulate MUC1 glycosylation and induce TnMUC1 antigen exposure
sec.p:
On the basis of these in vivo and in vitro experiments, we observed that EGFR TKIs enhanced the cytotoxicity of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells. The efficacy of many CAR-T cell therapies depends significantly on the expression levels of TSAs on target cells.30 To determine whether the cytotoxic effect of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells is influenced by TnMUC1 antigen expression, we manipulated membrane TnMUC1 levels in PC9 cells by overexpressing or knocking down MUC1. We then cocultured these modified PC9 cells with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells to assess cytotoxic activity. Our data showed that doubling TnMUC1 expression in PC9 cells significantly increased CAR-T cell cytotoxicity by more than 3-fold (Figures 3A–3D). Conversely, halving TnMUC1 expression reduced CAR-T cell cytotoxicity by approximately 50% (Figures 3E–3H). These findings highlight that TnMUC1 expression levels are a critical determinant of TnMUC1 CAR-T cell cytotoxicity.Figure 3

Given the interaction between EGFR and MUC1,31,32,33,34 we hypothesized that EGFR TKIs upregulated TnMUC1 antigen expression. TnMUC1 is a glycosylated peptide derived from the MUC1 glycoprotein, and its expression level depends on both MUC1 transcriptional activity and glycosylation status. To examine the relationship between MUC1 mRNA levels and TnMUC1 expression levels, we generated a correlation curve (Figure 3I). We modulated MUC1 mRNA levels in PC9 cells using different doses of MUC1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) or an overexpression plasmid and quantified TnMUC1 expression using flow cytometry. Our results showed that TnMUC1 expression remained relatively stable when MUC1 mRNA levels varied from 0.25- to 5-fold relative to the control. Additionally, quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) assays revealed that EGFR TKIs upregulated MUC1 mRNA expression but only modestly, with a maximum increase of 4-fold compared with the control (Figure 3J). Given the observed relationship between MUC1 mRNA and TnMUC1 expression, this limited transcriptional upregulation induced by EGFR TKIs appeared to be insufficient to directly enhance TnMUC1 expression.

To determine whether EGFR TKIs affect the glycosylation status of MUC1, we overexpressed FLAG-tagged MUC1 in PC9 cells and performed a pull-down assay to assess MUC1 glycosylation levels (Figure 3K). Our results showed that treatment with osimertinib reduced the smeared MUC1 protein band, which indicated a decrease in the MUC1 glycosylation level. In contrast, the 15-kDa MUC1-C domain, which was less glycosylated, remained unchanged. These findings suggested that EGFR TKIs inhibited MUC1 glycosylation. To further confirm this effect, we conducted a flow cytometry analysis of PC9 cells treated with osimertinib (Figures 3L and 3M) and erlotinib (Figures S7A and S7B) and revealed an upregulation of hypoglycosylated MUC1 (hMUC1) expression; glycosylated MUC1 (gMUC1) expression, however, remained largely unchanged. Additionally, we evaluated the expression scores of MUC1 O-glycosylation-related genes (MORGs) in tumor cells using published single-cell sequencing datasets.35 The analysis showed a significant downregulation of the MORG score in PC9 cells treated with erlotinib at the single-cell level (Figure 3N). Furthermore, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) analysis revealed an increased abundance of GalNAc modifications at Ser/Thr sites (Tn antigen) on multiple peptide segments in PC9 cells following osimertinib treatment (Figure S7C).

To evaluate TnMUC1 expression changes induced by EGFR TKI treatment, we performed flow cytometry analysis using the Tn218 antibody in EGFR-mutant PC9 and HCC827 cell lines. EGFR TKI exposure resulted in a more than 2-fold increase in TnMUC1 cell surface expression compared with untreated controls (Figures 3O, S7D, and S7E). We further confirmed this upregulation in vivo through IHC analysis of tumor bulks. Quantitative IHC scoring revealed a 3-fold elevation in TnMUC1 protein levels following EGFR TKI administration (Figures 3P, 3Q, S4D, and S4E). The observed TnMUC1 induction demonstrated model-independent consistency, which manifested in both CDXs and preclinical PDXs.

Given the upregulation of the tumor-specific TnMUC1 antigen by EGFR TKIs, we investigated changes in the tumor immune microenvironment following their administration. Building on the study by Gurule et al.,36 who analyzed biopsies from patients before and after 2 weeks of osimertinib treatment through transcriptional sequencing, we reanalyzed these specimens using the Tumor Immune Estimation Resource (TIMER) algorithm37 (Figure S8A). According to our analysis, most patients exhibited elevated immune scores after osimertinib treatment. Notably, dendritic cell and CD4+ T cell infiltration was enhanced, which suggested that EGFR TKIs may promote antitumor immune responses by facilitating TnMUC1 presentation to T cells through major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II molecules on antigen-presenting cells. To validate this hypothesis, we cocultured PC9 cells with PBMCs treated with osimertinib for 12 h. We then harvested the cells for immunoprecipitation analysis using a human leukocyte antigen-DR isotype (HLA-DR) antibody (Figure S8B), which confirmed that osimertinib enhanced HLA-DR-mediated presentation of TnMUC1. Furthermore, a reanalysis of the transcriptomic sequencing data from Gurule et al.36 revealed a general downregulation of glycosyltransferase expression after administering osimertinib (Figure S8C; Table S2). This finding supports our hypothesis that EGFR TKIs reduce MUC1 glycosylation, thereby upregulating TnMUC1 expression.

sec.title: EGFR TKIs induce TnMUC1 expression through C1GALT1 suppression
sec.p:
In this study, we synthesized the TnMUC1 antigen, a well-characterized TSA and therapeutic target for TnMUC1 CAR-T cells, through a defined biosynthetic pathway (Figure 4A).38,39,40,41,42,43,44 The pathway began with the addition of acetylgalactosamine to serine and threonine residues on the MUC1 peptide backbone and was catalyzed by N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferases (GALNTs) to generate the TnMUC1 antigen. Subsequently, C1GALT1 and C1GALT1C1 mediated the addition of galactose to TnMUC1, forming the Core1 glycan. B3GNT6 and GCNT1 further catalyzed the synthesis of Core3 and Core6 antigens, respectively. To investigate the impact of EGFR TKIs on TnMUC1 production, we analyzed the expression of glycosyltransferases involved in TnMUC1 biosynthesis in PC9 cells before and after osimertinib treatment (Figure 4B). Our results revealed a general upregulation of glycosyltransferases promoting TnMUC1 production and downregulation of those involved in TnMUC1 consumption following treatment. Notably, C1GALT1 exhibited the most pronounced reduction in mRNA expression, with an 80% decrease after osimertinib treatment. Western blot analysis further confirmed that both erlotinib and osimertinib significantly downregulated C1GALT1 protein expression (Figures 4C and 4D). Additionally, IHC analysis of clinical EGFR-mutant NSCLC samples revealed a negative correlation between C1GALT1 and TnMUC1 scores (Figures 4E and 4F). These data suggest that EGFR TKIs induce TnMUC1 expression by downregulating C1GALT1.

Next, we investigated the signaling pathway through which EGFR TKIs decreased C1GALT1 expression. EGFR activation typically stimulates the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) and phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K) pathways through its intracellular tyrosine kinase domain. To explore this process, we used EGFR-mutant PC9 cells for further investigation and EGFR wild-type A549 cells as the negative control. After treating the cells with osimertinib, we assessed the activation of the MAPK and PI3K pathways using western blot analysis (Figures S9A–S9D). Phosphorylated MEK (p-MEK) and p-ERK were used to evaluate MAPK pathway activation, while p-PI3K and p-AKT were used to assess PI3K pathway activation. The results showed that 8- and 24-h osimertinib treatments inhibited both MAPK and PI3K pathway activation in PC9 cells compared to A549 cells. To identify the predominant signaling pathway in this context, we treated PC9 cells with inhibitors targeting the MAPK (RAF, MEK, and ERK) and PI3K (PI3K and AKT) pathways and analyzed the expression patterns of TnMUC1-related glycosyltransferases (Figure 4G). The data revealed that the expression profile of TnMUC1-associated glycosyltransferases following PI3K pathway inhibition closely resembled that observed with osimertinib treatment. In contrast, treatment with MAPK pathway inhibitors resulted in a distinct expression pattern compared to osimertinib. These findings suggest that EGFR TKIs regulate C1GALT1 expression through the PI3K pathway, thereby influencing TnMUC1 expression. To confirm this hypothesis, we performed a rescue assay in PC9 cells using flow cytometry. PC9 cells were treated separately with osimertinib, PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitors (Figures 4H and 4I), and MAPK pathway inhibitors (Figures S9E and S9F), followed by overexpression of C1GALT1. The upregulation of TnMUC1 expression induced by EGFR TKIs and PI3K pathway inhibition was approximately 2-fold, which was completely reversed by C1GALT1 overexpression. In contrast, MAPK pathway inhibition did not increase TnMUC1 expression, and C1GALT1 overexpression could not rescue the effect. Additionally, C1GALT1 knockdown led to a 1-fold increase in TnMUC1 expression, and treatment with a PI3K/AKT pathway inhibitor did not further enhance this effect (Figures 4J and 4K). These findings confirm that EGFR TKIs regulate TnMUC1 expression by inhibiting C1GALT1 through the PI3K pathway.

sec.title: EGFR TKIs downregulate C1GALT1 transcription through PI3K/AKT/SP1 pathway inhibition
sec.p:
To predict transcription factors regulating C1GALT1, we used the JASPAR database to identify potential candidates (Figure S10A). We then analyzed their correlation with C1GALT1 expression using the lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) tumor dataset from GEPIA (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn/) (Figure 5A). We selected transcription factors with a Pearson correlation coefficient greater than 0.2 (SP1, ZNF460, ZNF770, and ZEB1) for further validation. To assess their regulatory roles, each transcription factor was individually knocked down, and we measured C1GALT1 expression by qPCR (Figures S10B and S10C) and western blot (Figures 5B, 5C, S10D, and S10E). Notably, SP1 knockdown reduced C1GALT1 expression by 50%, which was consistent with previous studies,46 whereas ZNF460, ZNF770, and ZEB1 knockdown had comparatively modest effects. Conversely, SP1 overexpression fully reversed the downregulation of C1GALT1 expression induced by erlotinib, osimertinib, PI3K inhibitors, and AKT inhibitors, as demonstrated by qPCR (Figure 5D) and western blot assays (Figures 5E–5G). These data demonstrate that SP1 plays a predominant role in the transcriptional regulation of C1GALT1 expression.Figure 5

To directly investigate the transcriptional activity of SP1 on C1GALT1, we employed dual-luciferase reporter gene assays and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)-PCR assays. These experiments revealed a 75% reduction in C1GALT1 transcriptional activity upon SP1 knockdown (Figure 5H). Notably, treatment with erlotinib, osimertinib, PI3K inhibitors, and AKT inhibitors similarly reduced C1GALT1 transcriptional activity, an effect that could be rescued by SP1 overexpression (Figure 5I). Furthermore, ChIP-PCR experiments using an anti-SP1 antibody demonstrated significant enrichment of DNA fragments in the C1GALT1 promoter region. This enrichment was reduced by 60% following treatment with EGFR TKIs and PI3K pathway inhibitors (Figure 5J). This result indicated that SP1 bound to the C1GALT1 promoter region and that this binding was attenuated by these inhibitors. To elucidate the direct interaction between SP1 and the PI3K/AKT pathway, we conducted coimmunoprecipitation (coIP) experiments (Figure 5K). The data revealed that SP1 interacts with p-AKT, the activated form of AKT kinase.47,48 Importantly, the binding of SP1 and p-AKT decreased after treatment with erlotinib or osimertinib. IHC analysis also revealed a significant positive correlation between C1GALT1 and SP1 expression scores in EGFR-mutant NSCLCs (Figures 5L and 5M).

These findings demonstrate that EGFR TKIs suppress C1GALT1 transcription by inhibiting the PI3K/AKT/SP1 pathway, further elucidating the mechanism by which EGFR TKIs regulate TnMUC1 antigen expression.

sec.title: C1GALT1 inhibitor mediates therapeutic sensitization to EGFR TKIs and enhances TnMUC1-targeted immunotherapy
sec.p:
C1GALT1 plays a crucial role as a glycosyltransferase in regulating MUC1 glycosylation. Inhibition of C1GALT1 function impedes MUC1 glycosylation, leading to the accumulation of the TnMUC1 antigen and enhancing the antitumor immune response, particularly the efficacy of TnMUC1 CAR-T cells. Recent studies have identified itraconazole as a natural inhibitor of C1GALT1, promoting its degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway.49 Western blot analysis confirmed that itraconazole reduced the protein level of C1GALT1 (Figures 6A and 6B), whereas mRNA expression levels of MUC1 and C1GALT1 remained unaffected (Figure 6C). To assess the impact of itraconazole on MUC1 glycosylation, we conducted flow cytometry on the EGFR-mutant PC9 cells and the EGFR wild-type A549 cells. The results demonstrated that itraconazole increased the expression of hMUC1 by more than 2-fold in PC9 cells and by more than 9-fold in A549 cells, independent of EGFR mutation status (Figures 6D and 6E), but it did not affect the expression of gMUC1 (Figures 6F and 6G). According to the flow cytometric analysis, itraconazole upregulated TnMUC1 expression on the surfaces of PC9 and A549 cells by more than 3-fold (Figures 6H and 6I). These findings suggest that combining itraconazole with EGFR TKIs may potentiate a stronger antitumor immune response by enhancing the expression of TnMUC1.Figure 6

To validate this hypothesis, we cocultured TnMUC1 CAR-T cells with PC9 cells. When cocultured with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells, treatment with either erlotinib or itraconazole alone enhanced cytotoxicity by over 2-fold, while their combination led to a nearly 10-fold increase (Figures S11A and S11B). We observed the same effect with the combined treatment of osimertinib and itraconazole in the coculture of PC9 and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells (Figures 6J and 6K). To further investigate the synergistic effects of itraconazole and EGFR TKIs on TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy, we established a subcutaneous tumor model using PC9 cells in NSG mice (Figures 6L and 6M). Our results demonstrated that tumors in the group receiving the combination of osimertinib, itraconazole, and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells were nearly eradicated. In the osimertinib plus TnMUC1 CAR-T group, tumor volumes decreased by approximately 70%, whereas in the itraconazole plus TnMUC1 CAR-T group, tumor volumes decreased by approximately 60%. These findings indicated that the combination of itraconazole, osimertinib, and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells significantly inhibited tumor growth. IHC analysis of the subcutaneous tumors revealed that both itraconazole and osimertinib downregulated C1GALT1 expression and upregulated TnMUC1 expression. We observed the most pronounced effect in the combination treatment group (Figures 6N and 6O). On the basis of these results, C1GALT1 inhibition by itraconazole may serve as a promising adjunctive therapy alongside EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The treatment landscape of NSCLC has evolved with targeted therapies and immunotherapies. EGFR TKIs show strong efficacy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, and ongoing studies are optimizing outcomes through first- to third-generation TKIs and their combinations with chemotherapy50,51 or ICIs.52

Despite these advances, NSCLC harboring driver gene mutations is often classified as a cold tumor, characterized by poor lymphocyte infiltration, a low tumor mutation burden, and weak immunogenicity, which collectively limit the effectiveness of immunotherapy in this subtype of lung cancer.

CAR-T cells offer a distinct therapeutic strategy by directly infiltrating tumor tissues, recognizing TSAs, and inducing tumor cell death. MUC1 has been extensively studied as a target for NSCLC immunotherapy. The interaction between EGFR and MUC1 has been implicated in tumor progression, which suggested that combining EGFR TKIs with MUC1-targeted CAR-T cells could enhance therapeutic efficacy. Among the various MUC1 CAR-T therapies, TnMUC1 has emerged as a particularly promising target because of its aberrant glycosylation in tumor cells.

In CAR-T cell therapy, efficacy largely depends on the availability of TSAs.26 We conducted an IHC analysis of tumor tissue samples from patients with NSCLC and found generally low TnMUC1 antigen expression, highlighting a key limitation of MUC1 CAR-T cell monotherapy in NSCLC. The results of our study, however, demonstrated that combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy both in vitro and in vivo. EGFR TKIs upregulated TnMUC1 expression, thereby improving the effectiveness of TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy. This strategy repurposed EGFR TKIs not as inhibitors of tumor growth through EGFR signaling but as enhancers of tumor-associated antigen MUC1 expression, thereby promoting TnMUC1 CAR-T recognition and cytotoxicity. This approach differentiates our work from traditional EGFR TKI applications and EGFR TKI and ICI combinations.

We investigated the effects of long-term osimertinib treatment combined with TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy in vivo, in particular following the development of osimertinib resistance. These results demonstrated significant tumor regression with this combination therapy, even after resistance developed. These findings suggest that combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy represents a promising therapeutic strategy for patients with EGFR TKI-resistant tumors. It remains unclear, however, whether re-administration of EGFR TKIs universally enhances TnMUC1 expression in the majority of post-resistant patients, which could further improve the combined efficacy with TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy. Additional studies involving diverse cell lines and preclinical models are necessary to validate this hypothesis and explore its broader applicability.

The safety concerns of combining EGFR TKIs with immunotherapy have been highlighted in studies involving ICIs. Current guidelines recommend against the use of ICIs in the first-line treatment of EGFR-mutant NSCLC. To address this limitation,8,53,54 we evaluated the safety of combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T therapy in PDXs. The results demonstrated no significant histopathological damage to major organs (e.g., heart, lungs, kidneys, or liver), and the treatment was well tolerated in mice (Figure S5). In contrast to the SAEs observed with EGFR TKI and ICI combinations, which arise from (1) overlapping toxicities in organs, such as the skin and gastrointestinal tract,11,12 and (2) EGFR TKI-mediated inhibition of hepatic drug-metabolizing enzymes, leading to impaired ICI clearance and hepatotoxicity,13,14 these mechanisms are absent in CAR-T therapy because of its distinct pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles. This result provides a theoretical basis for the improved safety of combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy.

Mechanistically, EGFR TKIs upregulate TnMUC1 by suppressing C1GALT1 via the EGFR/PI3K/AKT/SP1 pathway, thereby enhancing CAR-T cell recognition and cytotoxicity (Figure S11C). Given the widespread activation of PI3K/AKT in various cancers—including breast, head and neck, and colorectal—targeting this pathway may further increase TnMUC1 expression and potentiate TnMUC1-based immunotherapies.

Our research has underscored the pivotal role of C1GALT1 in TnMUC1 formation. Alterations in C1GALT1 expression can significantly affect the glycosylation of various cell membrane glycoproteins, including mucins. Elevated C1GALT1 expression has been associated with cancer progression and poor prognosis in LUAD and gastric cancer tissues.46,55 We found that itraconazole, a C1GALT1 inhibitor, reduced MUC1 glycosylation and enhanced TnMUC1 antigen expression. As a broad-spectrum antifungal agent, itraconazole is not restricted by EGFR mutation status and offers advantages such as minimal side effects and broad clinical applicability. Thus, itraconazole holds promise as a sensitizer for EGFR TKIs or TnMUC1 CAR-T cells in solid tumors by enhancing TnMUC1 expression.

In our study, the absence of a commercially available antibody specifically targeting TnMUC1 posed a challenge. To address this, we employed the Tn218 monoclonal antibody to detect TnMUC1 expression. Tn218, developed using aOSM, selectively binds to the Tn antigen on MUC1, as confirmed by our pull-down assay (Figure S2). In the future, however, the development of a commercially available TnMUC1 antibody would allow for more definitive validation of EGFR TKI-mediated TnMUC1 upregulation.

In this study, we proposed combining EGFR TKIs with TnMUC1 CAR-T therapy to address the limitations of targeted therapy and immunotherapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC. This strategy is promising for enhancing therapeutic efficacy and improving clinical outcomes. Further investigations and rigorous clinical trials, however, are required to validate its efficacy and safety.

sec.title: Limitations of the study
sec.p: Although our study demonstrated that EGFR TKIs potentiate the efficacy of TnMUC1 CAR-T cell therapy in EGFR-mutant NSCLC, several limitations warrant consideration. Most notably, although we observed robust preclinical efficacy, the clinical relevance of combining EGFR TKIs and TnMUC1 CAR-T cells remains to be established in prospective human trials. In addition, although preliminary safety assessments in PDXs did not reveal any major organ toxicities, comprehensive evaluation in long-term, immunocompetent models is necessary to fully characterize potential immune-related risks. Furthermore, because of the lack of a commercially available antibody specific for TnMUC1, antigen detection relied on the Tn218 monoclonal antibody, which, although validated for specificity, may not capture the full heterogeneity of TnMUC1 expression induced by EGFR TKIs. Future studies addressing these limitations are critical for translating this combinatorial approach into clinical practice.

sec.title: Experimental model and study participant details
Clinical specimens
sec.p: The TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T cells used in this study were prepared and provided by Guangzhou Anjie Biomedical Technology Co., Ltd. (Guangzhou, China). Whole peripheral blood was collected from patients, who provided informed consent before participation in this study. The Ethics Committee of Sun Yat-sen Memorial Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University (Approval No. 2019-KY-001) approved the study. Detailed information is given in Table S1. sec.title: Cell lines and cell culture
sec.p: We acquired PC9, HCC827, and A549 from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Osimertinib-resistant HCC827 cells were generated by exposing cells to 100 nM osimertinib for 30 days. We cultured cell lines in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI)-1640 media supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) in humidified 5% CO2 incubator at 37°C. To verify origin, we subjected cell lines to short-tandem repeat (STR) detection.

sec.title: Animals
sec.p: We conducted animal studies using female NSG mice aged 6 to 12 weeks, which we obtained from Shanghai Model Organisms and housed in a specific-pathogen-free (SPF) environment in a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle. Food and purified water were freely available to all mice in this study. Mice were randomly assigned to experimental groups. The Animal Care and Use Committee of Sun Yat-Sen University approved the CDX model animal protocols (Approval Number: 2024000374). Animal care was handled in accordance with the Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals of the Guangdong Laboratory Animal Monitoring Institute. The Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (Approval numbers: SYSU-IACUC-2024-001179 and IACUC2020115) approved the experimental procedures.

We obtained PDX models from Innomodels Inc. (Beijing, China). We collected tumor surgical samples with informed patient consent, cut into 2 mm × 2 mm fragments, and transplanted subcutaneously into immunodeficient NSG mice within 30 min, without the use of Matrigel or other additives. Tumors smaller than 1,000 mm3 were excised and passaged into additional NSG mice for further study. The construction of the PDX model was approved by the Ethics Committee for Life Ethics (Approval Numbers: IACUC-005-2024-0079 and IACUC-005-2024-0001).

sec.title: CAR-T cell preparation
sec.p: Guangzhou Anjie Biomedical Technology Co. Ltd. (Guangzhou, China) prepared and supplied the TnMUC1-targeted CAR-T cells used in this study. We collected whole peripheral blood from patients. We constructed second-generation TnMUC1 CARs using scFv derived from antibody clones 5E5, hinge and transmembrane regions from CD8α, intracellular domain from CD137, and intracellular domain from CD247 (CD3-zeta). We isolated PBMCs from 60 to 80 mL of peripheral blood from donors by centrifugation on a Ficoll density gradient. We cultured PBMCs in KBM581 medium supplemented with anti-CD3 antibody, recombinant human IL-2, and 5% heat-inactivated self-serum. One day after anti-CD3antibody stimulation, T cells were transduced with lentiviral vector containing TnMUC1-CAR and maintained in media supplemented with IL-2. We performed gene editing by electroporation of CasRNPs, which were prepared immediately before the experiments by incubating 20 μg Cas9 (Guangzhou Anjie Biomedical Technology Co. Ltd.) at 37°C for 10 min. CasRNPs were electroporated in cells using a BTX830 (Harvard Apparatus BTX). Following electroporation, cells were immediately placed in prewarmed culture medium and cultured at 37°C and 5% CO2. We replaced half of the cell culture medium every two to three days. Cell density was adjusted to 2 × 106 cells per milliliter. We quantified surface expression of CARs using flow cytometry. CAR expression analysis revealed CAR copy numbers less than five copies per cell according to qPCR, whereas flow cytometry confirmed CAR-positive rates ≥20% across all batches except Donor 15 (11.3%), exceeding the ≥10% acceptance threshold. T cell viability metrics showed CD3-positive rates ≥94%, cell viability ≥90%, and IFN-γ release levels ≥0.72 ng/mL (surpassing the 0.5 ng/mL critical value), which collectively indicated robust T cell activation and functionality. Final products exhibited homogeneous yellowish suspensions without particulates, standardized volumes of 100 mL, and pH values within the optimal culture medium range (7.0–7.5). Total cell counts and CAR-positive cell counts aligned with predefined specifications (Table S1).

sec.title: Animal experiment
sec.p: We suspended 5 × 106 wild-type PC9 and HCC827 cells, along with osimertinib-resistant HCC827 cells, in 100 μL of Matrigel and injected them subcutaneously into the backs of NSG mice to establish CDX models. Once the CDX tumors became palpable or the PDX tumors reached a volume of approximately 100 mm3, we administered erlotinib (20 mg/kg) or osimertinib (20 mg/kg) or itraconazole (40 mg/kg) orally every three days. On the second day following the first EGFR TKI administration, we injected either 5 × 107 TnMUC1 CAR-T cells or PBMCs were injected through the tail vein. We calculated tumor volume using the following formula: V (mm3) = 0.5 × (length × width2). We harvested, weighed, and formalin-fixed xenografts upon observing significant differences in tumor volume among groups or when the smallest tumors were no longer detectable.

sec.title: Real-time quantitative reverse transcription PCR
sec.p: We extracted total RNA from cultured cells using standard protocols. Briefly, cells were lysed with Trizol, followed by chloroform addition and centrifugation to separate the aqueous phase containing RNA. The aqueous phase was then transferred to a new tube, mixed with isopropanol to precipitate the RNA, and centrifuged. We washed the resulting RNA pellet with 75% ethanol, and then we air-dried and dissolved it in DEPC-treated water or RNA dissolution buffer. Total RNA was reverse-transcribed into cDNA using the PrimeScript RT reagent kit. The reaction mixture contained 500 ng of RNA, 5× PrimeScript Buffer, and DEPC-treated water. We performed reverse transcription at 37°C for 15 min. We conducted real-time quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) using the SYBR Premix Ex Taq II kit on a LightCycler 480 System (Roche, Basel, Switzerland). The reaction mixture included cDNA, primers, TB Green Premix Ex Taq II (2×), and DEPC-treated water. The qPCR conditions consisted of predenaturation at 95°C for 30 s, followed by 40 cycles of amplification at 95°C for 3 s and 60°C for 30 s.

sec.title: Immunoblotting
sec.p: We used RIPA buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors for cell lysis. We separated protein samples by 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) and transferred onto polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. Membranes were blocked with 5% nonfat milk in 0.1% TBST for 1 h, followed by incubation with primary antibodies and second antibodies (1:500 to 1:1000) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. We detected protein–antibody complexes using horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-conjugated secondary antibodies and enhanced chemiluminescence. Bands were visualized with the ChemiDoc MP Imaging System (Bio-Rad, Hercules, CA, USA). We analyzed western blot bands using ImageJ software. We removed background noise before selecting the bands and measuring grayscale intensity. We calculated the relative intensity ratio by dividing the grayscale intensity of the target protein band by that of the internal control band.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: PC9 or HCC827 cells were cocultured with PBMCs or TnMUC1 CAR-T cells at an E:T ratio of 5:1. After treatment with 1 μM osimertinib or erlotinib for 8 h, we collected cells from the coculture. PC9 and HCC827 cells were dissociated into single-cell suspensions in PBS and incubated with flow cytometry antibodies (diluted 1:100 to 1:200) for 30 min, following the manufacturer’s instructions. After washing with PBS, the cells were resuspended in 300 μL of PBS for flow cytometry analysis. To detect hypoglycosylated MUC1 (hMUC1), we used the anti-SM3 antibody.56,57 We identified glycosylated MUC1 (gMUC1) using the anti-16A antibody,58 and we detected the TnMUC1 antigen with the anti-Tn218 antibody.

Propidium iodide (PI) and calcein-AM are used to detect the cell viability and the status of cell life and death of tumor cells cocultured with T cells. Calcein-AM-labeled tumor cells were cocultured with TnMUC1 CAR-T cells or PBMCs for 8 h at an effector-to-target ratio of 5:1, with or without 1 μM erlotinib or 1 μM osimertinib treatment, and maintained in 24-well plates. Following coculture, mixed cells were stained with PI and analyzed using flow cytometry. We identified dead tumor cells as calcein-AM and PI double-positive cells. In a parallel experiment, tumor cells were cocultured with PBMCs or TnMUC1 CAR-T cells under the same conditions. After incubation, cells were stained with CD45 to distinguish immune cells and calcein-AM to mark tumor cells. We identified viable tumor cells as CD45-negative and calcein-AM-positive cells.

We measured fluorescence intensity for each sample using NovoCyte cytometer (Agilent Technologies Santa Clara, CA, USA) and performed an analysis with FlowJo software v10 (FlowJo, LLC, Ashland, OR, USA).

sec.title: O-glycosylation analysis
sec.p: We treated PC9 cells with or without 1 μM osimertinib for 8 h, after which we sent the samples to Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) for protein O-glycosylation analysis. Briefly, we subjected immunoprecipitated MUC1 from PC9 cells to SDS-PAGE and excised the corresponding bands. The proteins were reduced with DTT, alkylated with iodoacetamide, and digested with trypsin overnight. We then analyzed the digested peptides using LC-MS/MS, performed on a nanoAcquity (Waters Corp., Milford, MA, USA) coupled to an LTQ Orbitrap Velos (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). We operated the LTQ Orbitrap Velos in the data-dependent mode and selected the 10 most intense precursors for collision-induced dissociation (CID) fragmentation. Raw data files were processed using Proteome Discoverer (PD) version 2.0 (Thermo Scientific). We analyzed the peak lists using Sequest against the Homo sapiens Uniprot database. We applied the following parameters for tryptic peptide identification: precursor ion mass tolerance (10 ppm); product ion mass tolerance (0.6 Da); and missed trypsin cleavage sites (up to 2). Fixed modifications were carbamidomethylation of Cys; variable modifications were oxidation of Met and phosphorylation of Ser/Thr; and O-linked GalNAc modification were +197.118 Da at Ser/Thr.

sec.title: T cell activation experiment
sec.p: We isolated PBMCs from human peripheral blood and cultured the samples overnight in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS. We collected suspended lymphocytes and discarded adherent cells. The lymphocytes were subsequently activated for 12 h in DMEM containing 10% FBS and human IL-2 using T cell TransAct reagent at a 1:100 dilution. We treated lymphocytes with 1 μM erlotinib or osimertinib. We used flow cytometry to quantify the proportions of activated CD8+CD25+ and CD8+CD69+ T cells. We measured IFN-γ and IL-2 in the culture medium using ELISA.

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
sec.p: For the tumor tissue analysis, we dissected subcutaneous tumors from the PDXs, flash-froze the samples in liquid nitrogen, and homogenized the samples in RIPA lysis buffer. After lysis for 30 min, centrifuged samples at 12,000 rpm at 4°C for 20 min. We collected the supernatant for ELISA to quantify IFN-γ production by TnMUC1 CAR-T cells or PBMCs within the tumor tissue. We determined protein concentration using the bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay to normalize ELISA results.

For the coculture supernatant analysis, we collected the supernatant from the coculture system for ELISA to measure IFN-γ, IL-2, GZMB, IL-10, and TGF-β levels and assessed cytokine production by TnMUC1 CAR–T cells or PBMCs in vitro. Briefly, we added 100 µL of the standard or sample to each well of a microplate, followed by 50 µL of biotinylated antibody. We incubated the plate at room temperature for 2 h and then washed it. Next, we added 100 µL of streptavidin-HRP working solution to each well and incubated it at room temperature for 20 min, followed by another wash. Subsequently, we added 100 µL of TMB substrate and incubated the plate in the dark at room temperature for 10–20 min. We stopped the reaction within 10 min and measured absorbance at 450 nm (measurement) and 610–630 nm (reference).

sec.title: Immunohistochemistry
sec.p: We performed IHC according to standard protocols. After dewaxing and rehydration, we blocked endogenous peroxidase activity using 3% hydrogen peroxide. The slides were then incubated with 10% goat serum for blocking. We applied primary antibodies against CD3, TnMUC1, C1GALT1, and SP1, followed by overnight incubation at 4°C. The IHC secondary antibody was then applied at room temperature for 30 min. We conducted signal detection using the diaminobenzidine (DAB) detection kit. We visualized immunostaining using an Olympus BX51 microscope (Olympus, Tokyo, Japan). We assessed staining scores based on the proportion of positively stained areas in three randomly selected fields under a 20× objective. The scoring criteria were as follows: 0, no positively stained area; 1, <25% stained area; 2, 25–50% stained area; and 3, >50% stained area.

sec.title: Luciferase reporter assay
sec.p: We seeded PC9 cells in 12-well plates at a density of 4 × 105 cells per well and cotransfected the cells with a mixture of 0.8 μg pGL3.1 vector containing the C1GALT1 promoter or the pGL3.1 basic control plasmid, along with 0.8 μg pcDNA3.1-SP1 or the corresponding control plasmid, using Lipofectamine 3000 according to the manufacturer’s protocol. We included the pRL-TK plasmid as a control for transfection efficiency. After 48 h, cells were lysed, and the lysates were collected. We measured the Firefly and Renilla luciferase activities using the Dual-Luciferase Reporter Assay System. Relative firefly luciferase activity was normalized to Renilla luciferase activity. We detected luminescence using a microplate reader (SuPerMax 3100, Shanghai, China).

sec.title: Chromatin immunoprecipitation
sec.p: We conducted ChIP assays using the EZ-ChIP kit according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, we cross-linked PC9 cells with formaldehyde and lysed the cells to release chromatin. SP1 and its associated chromatin fragments were immunoprecipitated using SP1 antibodies conjugated to magnetic beads, thereby enriching chromatin bound by SP1. After multiple washes to remove nonspecifically bound materials, the precipitated chromatin was decrosslinked to release DNA fragments. We used the following ChIP primers targeting the C1GALT1 promoter sequences:
GCTGAGAATCCCACTCAAGGT.
CATGAGCCTCAGAATGCCAG.
We quantified immunoprecipitated DNA using real-time qPCR and normalized the ChIP data to input DNA using the formula: 2[Input Ct - Target Ct] × 0.1 × 100%.

sec.title: Coimmunoprecipitation
sec.p: We lysed cells using Pierce IP Lysis Buffer. We immunoprecipitated the lysates with the indicated SP1 antibodies. We added protein A/G beads to the mixture, which was then incubated overnight at 4°C with rotation. Eluted proteins were boiled in SDS buffer and analyzed by western blotting.

sec.title: Pulldown assay
sec.p: FLAG-tagged MUC1 was overexpressed in PC9 or HCC827 cells. The cells were lysed using Pierce IP Lysis Buffer, and the lysates were immunoprecipitated with the indicated FLAG antibodies on protein A/G beads overnight at 4°C with rotation. We washed the proteins bound to the beads three times. After we eluted the proteins, they were boiled in SDS buffer and analyzed by western blot.

sec.title: Gene Expression Omnibus datasets and data processing
sec.p: We obtained raw gene expression profiling data for lung cancer from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/). Specifically, we downloaded transcriptomic data from GEO: GSE165019,20 focusing on tumor biopsies from eight patients with EGFR-mutant lung cancer before and after two weeks of osimertinib treatment. We processed the datasets using the GPL10588 platform. We identified differentially expressed MORGs using the limma package in R.

sec.title: Expression analysis of MORGs in single cell level
sec.p: We obtained gene expression data from the GEO dataset GEO: GSE134836.35 We performed single-cell data processing using Seurat. We excluded genes expressed in fewer than 25 cells, cells with fewer than 500 or more than 6000 detected genes, mitochondrial gene proportions exceeding 30%, ribosomal gene proportions exceeding 3%, and hemoglobin gene proportions below 10% were excluded. We identified and removed doublets using the DoubletFinder package. The expression matrix was normalized with the NormalizeData function in Seurat. We filtered out cells that lacked MUC1 expression and classified the remaining cells into Day0 and Day3 groups based on experimental conditions. Genes related to the 'Mucin type O-glycan biosynthesis–Homo sapiens (human)' pathway (hsa00512) were extracted from the KEGG database. We used the gsva function in the GSVA package to calculate gene expression scores for the hsa00512 pathway in the Day0 and Day3 groups. We conducted data visualization using ggplot2.

sec.title: Quantification and statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism 7 software (GraphPad Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA). For most in vitro and in vivo experiments, we calculated P-values using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-tests. We applied post hoc analyses (e.g., Tukey’s test) for intergroup comparisons. Results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from three or more independent replicates. We defined statistical significance thresholds as follows: ∗p < 0.05, ∗∗p < 0.01, ∗∗∗p < 0.001, and ∗∗∗∗p < 0.0001.
